newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian opposition leader rallies resistance.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian opposition leader rallies resistance.

text.p: A leader of Cambodia's embattled opposition arrived on the Thai-Cambodian on Tuesday to rally resistance to strongman Hun Sen nine days after the ouster of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh.

Sam Rainsy, a former finance minister and ally of Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party, said he had returned from Europe to help followers who fled to the border after Ranariddh's bloody overthrow on July 6.
Sam Rainsy was expelled from the National Assembly in late 1994 after he upset powerful political figures with his campaign against corruption.
"I told my people to resist as a matter of principle...to fight against (Second Prime Minister) Hun Sen," he told Reuters in the Thai border town of Aranyaprathet.
"We have agreed to join the resistance with the FUNCINPEC.

"Before I came here I met with Prince Ranariddh and his message to FUNCINPEC is to resist against the dictatorship," he said. "This is not a matter of (political) parties but it's a matter of the nation."
Forces under Hun Sen have pushed troops loyal to Ranariddh back into the jungles of northern Cambodia in clashes over recent days.

Indonesia said on Tuesday that foreign ministers from Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines would meet Ranariddh's father, King Norodom Sihanouk, in Beijing on Thursday to discuss the crisis. Sihanouk has been in the Chinese capital for medical treatment.

They will meet Sihanouk as a committee representing the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN), which has postponed Cambodia's membership of the seven-nation organisation due to the current turmoil. Cambodia had been due to join this month.
Australia halted military aid to Cambodia on Tuesday to step up pressure on Hun Sen to restore constitutional rule and honour a pledge to hold a free and fair election next May.
The United States had already suspended aid to Cambodia for 30 days.
Hun Sen said on Monday that big powers should not use aid as a weapon to threaten him and he condemned outside interference in Cambodia's affairs.

But he has gone to great lengths to try to justify his action against Ranariddh, who left the country shortly before fighting broke out in the capital but has vowed to lead resistance against Hun Sen.

At least 58 people were killed and up to 200 wounded, most of them civilians caught in the crossfire as the two sides battled in Phnom Penh for two days after Hun sen's men moved against forces loyal to Ranariddh.

Last week the foreign ministry published a white paper giving details of Ranariddh's "strategy of provocation" including his attempts to strengthen his forces with defectors from the dreaded Khmer Rouge guerrilla group and arm them with smuggled weapons.

Hun Sen denied staging a coup against Ranariddh. He said he had to take action against Ranariddh's military commanders because they were bringing "illegal forces" and weapons into Phnom Penh to bolster the prince's troop strength.
Ranariddh denied his commanders were smuggling Khmer Rouge defectors into the city.

Four rebel defectors told a news conference organised by the ministry of information on Tuesday that Ranariddh's top military commander had infiltrated Khmer Rouge defectors into the capital for a planned coup against Hun Sen.
They said Ranariddh's top commander, General Nhiek Bun Chhay, had plans to bring 10,000 Khmer Rouge fighters to Phnom Penh.

"Nhiek Bun Chhay wanted to bring 10,000 Khmer Rouge to Phnom Penh and 1,600 to Kompong Cham in order to fight and take power from...Hun Sen," one of the defectors, Phon Peap, told the news conference.
Kompong Cham is a province just to the north of Phnom Penh.
The Khmer Rouge, responsible for the death of a million people during their 1975-79 rule, has been hit by a wave of defections in recent years.
Both prime ministers tried to lure defecting guerrillas to their side as a power-sharing row between them worsened and their unwieldly coalition government came under strain.

Ranariddh won a U.N.-supervised election in 1993 but agreed to the coalition after Hun Sen, the leader of Cambodia's former communist government, objected to the poll result and the country faced divison along factional lines.
